This includes checking for common security vulnerabilities, validating input handling, reviewing authentication/authorization implementations, scanning for hardcoded secrets, and ensuring OWASP compliance. <example>Context: The user wants to ensure their newly implemented API endpoints are secure before deployment.
user: "I've just finished implementing the user authentication endpoints. Can you check them for security issues?"
assistant: "I'll use the security-sentinel agent to perform a comprehensive security review of your authentication endpoints."
<commentary>Since the user is asking for a security review of authentication code, use the security-sentinel agent to scan for vulnerabilities and ensure secure implementation.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user is concerned about potential SQL injection vulnerabilities in their database queries.
user: "I'm worried about SQL injection in our search functionality. Can you review it?"
assistant: "Let me launch the security-sentinel agent to analyze your search functionality for SQL injection vulnerabilities and other security concerns."
<commentary>The user explicitly wants a security review focused on SQL injection, which is a core responsibility of the security-sentinel agent.</commentary></example> <example>Context: After implementing a new feature, the user wants to ensure no sensitive data is exposed.
user: "I've added the payment processing module. Please check if any sensitive data might be exposed."
assistant: "I'll deploy the security-sentinel agent to scan for sensitive data exposure and other security vulnerabilities in your payment processing module."
<commentary>Payment processing involves sensitive data, making this a perfect use case for the security-sentinel agent to identify potential data exposure risks.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:bug-reproduction-validator: Use this agent when you receive a bug report or issue description and need to verify whether the reported behavior is actually a bug. This agent will attempt to reproduce the issue systematically, validate the steps to reproduce, and confirm whether the behavior deviates from expected functionality. <example>
Context: The user has reported a potential bug in the application.
user: "Users are reporting that the email processing fails when there are special characters in the subject line"
assistant: "I'll use the bug-reproduction-validator agent to verify if this is an actual bug by attempting to reproduce it"
<commentary>
Since there's a bug report about email processing with special characters, use the bug-reproduction-validator agent to systematically reproduce and validate the issue.
</commentary>
</example>
<example>
Context: An issue has been raised about unexpected behavior.
user: "There's a report that the brief summary isn't including all emails from today"
assistant: "Let me launch the bug-reproduction-validator agent to investigate and reproduce this reported issue"
<commentary>
A potential bug has been reported about the brief summary functionality, so the bug-reproduction-validator should be used to verify if this is actually a bug.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:every-style-editor: Use this agent when you need to review and edit text content to conform to Every's specific style guide. This includes reviewing articles, blog posts, newsletters, documentation, or any written content that needs to follow Every's editorial standards. The agent will systematically check for title case in headlines, sentence case elsewhere, company singular/plural usage, overused words, passive voice, number formatting, punctuation rules, and other style guide requirements. (Tools: Task, Glob, Grep, LS, ExitPlanMode, Read, Edit, MultiEdit, Write, NotebookRead, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch)
- entire-engineering:workflow:lint: Use this agent when you need to run linting and code quality checks on Ruby and ERB files. Run before pushing to origin. (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:pr-comment-resolver: Use this agent when you need to address comments on pull requests or code reviews by making the requested changes and reporting back on the resolution. This agent handles the full workflow of understanding the comment, implementing the fix, and providing a clear summary of what was done. <example>Context: A reviewer has left a comment on a pull request asking for a specific change to be made.user: "The reviewer commented that we should add error handling to the payment processing method"assistant: "I'll use the pr-comment-resolver agent to address this comment by implementing the error handling and reporting back"<commentary>Since there's a PR comment that needs to be addressed with code changes, use the pr-comment-resolver agent to handle the implementation and resolution.</commentary></example><example>Context: Multiple code review comments need to be addressed systematically.user: "Can you fix the issues mentioned in the code review? They want better variable names and to extract the validation logic"assistant: "Let me use the pr-comment-resolver agent to address these review comments one by one"<commentary>The user wants to resolve code review feedback, so the pr-comment-resolver agent should handle making the changes and reporting on each resolution.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:spec-flow-analyzer: Use this agent when you have a specification, plan, feature description, or technical document that needs user flow analysis and gap identification. This agent should be used proactively when:

<example>
Context: The user has just finished drafting a specification for OAuth implementation.
user: "Here's the OAuth spec for our new integration:
[OAuth spec details]"
assistant: "Let me use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to analyze this OAuth specification for user flows and missing elements."
<commentary>
Since the user has provided a specification document, use the Task tool to launch the spec-flow-analyzer agent to identify all user flows, edge cases, and missing clarifications.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: The user is planning a new social sharing feature.
user: "I'm thinking we should add social sharing to posts. Users can share to Twitter, Facebook, and LinkedIn."
assistant: "This sounds like a feature specification that would benefit from flow analysis. Let me use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to map out all the user flows and identify any missing pieces."
<commentary>
The user is describing a new feature. Use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to analyze the feature from the user's perspective, identify all permutations, and surface questions about missing elements.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: The user has created a plan for a new onboarding flow.
user: "Can you review this onboarding plan and make sure we haven't missed anything?"
assistant: "I'll use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to thoroughly analyze this onboarding plan from the user's perspective."
<commentary>
The user is explicitly asking for review of a plan. Use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to identify all user flows, edge cases, and gaps in the specification.
</commentary>
</example>

Call this agent when:
- A user presents a feature specification, plan, or requirements document
- A user asks to review or validate a design or implementation plan
- A user describes a new feature or integration that needs flow analysis
- After initial planning sessions to validate completeness
- Before implementation begins on complex user-facing features
- When stakeholders need clarity on user journeys and edge cases (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- posthog:error-analyzer: Analyze multiple PostHog errors in parallel to identify patterns, root causes, and prioritize fixes based on user impact. (Tools: All tools)
- reviewer: Code review agent - critically reviews changes for quality, security, and correctness (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- test-doc: Use this agent when the user needs markdown files created in the test-files/ directory. This includes generating test data files, sample documentation, mock content, or any markdown-formatted files for testing purposes.

Examples:

<example>
Context: User needs sample markdown files for testing a documentation parser.
user: "I need some sample markdown files to test my parser"
assistant: "I'll use the markdown-file-generator agent to create sample markdown files in the test-files/ directory for your parser testing."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example>

Context: User is setting up test fixtures and needs markdown content.
user: "Create a few test markdown files with different heading levels and formatting"
assistant: "Let me use the markdown-file-generator agent to create markdown files with varied formatting in the test-files/ directory."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: User needs mock README files for testing.
user: "Generate some fake README files for my test suite"
assistant: "I'll invoke the markdown-file-generator agent to create mock README files in the test-files/ directory."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

## plugin:entire-engineering:context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

- diagnose: Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Reproduce → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test. Use when user says "diagnose this" / "debug this", reports a bug, says something is broken/throwing/failing, or describes a performance regression.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- github-triage: Triage GitHub issues through a label-based state machine. Use when user wants to create an issue, triage issues, review incoming bugs or feature requests, prepare issues for an AFK agent, or manage issue workflow.
- review-pr-feedback: Walk every unresolved review thread on the current branch's PR — fix what is fixable, ask the user about anything ambiguous, then reply on each thread and mark it resolved. Use when the user says "review PR feedback", "go thru the PR comments", "address review comments", or similar.
- ship: Commit, push, and update the PR description or add a comment based on new changes. Use when the user says "ship it", "commit push and update pr", or similar.
- to-issues: Break a plan, spec, or PRD into independently-grabbable GitHub issues using tracer-bullet vertical slices. Use when user wants to convert a plan into issues, create implementation tickets, or break down work into issues.
- to-prd: Turn the current conversation context into a PRD and submit it as a GitHub issue. Use when user wants to create a PRD from the current context.
- unslop: Cut AI tells from any writing. Must always apply.
- write-a-skill: Create new agent skills with proper structure, progressive disclosure, and bundled resources. Use when user wants to create, write, or build a new skill.
- agent-integration: Run all three agent integration phases sequentially: research, write-tests, and implement using E2E-first TDD (unit tests written last). For individual phases, use /agent-integration:research, /agent-integration:write-tests, or /agent-integration:implement. Use when the user says "integrate agent", "add agent support", or wants to run the full agent integration pipeline end-to-end.
- changelog: Generate or update the CHANGELOG.md for a new release version. Use when the user says "generate changelog", "update changelog", "write release notes", or asks to prepare a changelog for a version like "changelog for 0.5.3".
- e2e: Orchestrate E2E test triage and fix implementation: runs triage-ci then implement sequentially. Accepts test names, --agent, artifact path, or CI run reference. For individual phases, use /e2e:triage-ci, /e2e:debug, or /e2e:implement. Use when the user says "triage e2e", "fix e2e failures", or wants the full triage-to-fix pipeline.
- test-repo: Use this skill to test strategy changes against a fresh test repository. Invoke when the user asks to "test against a test repo", "validate the changes", or wants to verify session hooks, commits, and rewind functionality work correctly.

You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. content.content:
Finding:   01M0FJ6N8PS0Z89XYMXNJP4JTQ
Status:    open
Freshness: current
Severity:  medium
Confidence: 0.85
Location: cmd/entire/cli/remote_topology.go:115

The note can name a remote whose checkpoints do not go there (dedicated checkpoint_remote mode)

`describeSyncRemote` (remote_topology.go:229) prints `t.syncRemote` without consulting `pinned`, while the block that calls it (remote_topology.go:196-199) enumerates only *unpinned* remotes. When the elected remote is pinned — `checkpoint_remote` in effect for it — the note names a destination that is neither in the list it just printed nor where checkpoints actually go.

Reproduced against the real functions with a temporary test (no unit test currently reaches `describeCheckpointDestination`), destinations `colleague`, `origin` (pinned), `upstream`, syncRemote `origin`, source `default`:

    Checkpoint destination: REVIEW
      This repo has 2 remotes (colleague, upstream).
        Checkpoints sync to one remote — right now "origin". A push to a different
        remote of your own can move it; `entire status` shows where they go.
        Set strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote to pin one yourself.

Two remotes listed, a third named as the destination. And `pinned` for the elected remote is exactly the predicate that makes `entire status` print `Checkpoints sync to: dedicated checkpoint remote (<repo>)` — status.go:290-305 requires `GetCheckpointRemote() != nil` plus `PushURL(elected)` enabled, both implied by `pinned`, since `PushURL` returns `enabled=false` when the config is nil. So `enable`/`doctor` name `origin` while `status` names the dedicated store.

Reachable in a mixed-ownership fork setup: `checkpoint_remote` set, `origin` = your fork (ownership matches -> pinned), `upstream` plus a colleague's remote (`checkpointRemoteIsInherited` -> unpinned).

Root cause: `inspectRemoteTopology:115` calls `strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` directly, bypassing `computeCheckpointSyncInfo`, which status.go:259 documents as "the single shared computation behind both the text and JSON checkpoint-sync sections … so the two outputs cannot drift" and which already handles dedicated mode. Three surfaces now read one election and only two share code; the one that opted out is the one that drifted. Routing the note through it also yields the `Err` string for free — the only mismatch is its `CountUnpushedCheckpoints` call, which the note does not need, so splitting the count off would let all three share the destination logic. The PR's own reason for asking the resolver ("the same rule `pinned` follows") argues for this: `pinned` asks `remote.PushURL` precisely because a *present* `checkpoint_remote` is not necessarily *in effect*.

Verified on f9eb943f3: gofmt clean, `golangci-lint run ./cmd/entire/cli/...` 0 issues, `TestDescribeSyncRemote` and `TestMultiPushURL` (integration) all pass — this state is unreachable from either, since the unit table sets no `destinations` and the integration repo configures no `checkpoint_remote`.

content.text:
That output is expected — and it confirms the finding is unreachable, which is why it's dismissed/stale.

Two things are going on:

**1. With one remote the note is never printed at all.** `describeCheckpointDestination` returns early on `!t.ambiguous()` (`remote_topology.go:161`), and `ambiguous()` is only true if some remote fans out to >1 push URL, or if **more than one** unpinned remote exists (`:145-157`). One remote, one URL → nothing. On top of that, the `describeSyncRemote` call is itself behind `if names := t.unpinnedNames(); len(names) > 1` (`:196`). So the Sole arm can't be reached from this caller — the code comment at `:260-264` says exactly that ("Sole is all but unreachable from this caller… the two count remotes with different git commands, so the arm stays shared rather than assert an impossibility").

**2. The wording the finding quotes no longer exists.** The shared Default/Sole/First arm now reads:

```
Checkpoints sync to one remote — right now "origin". A push to a different
remote of your own can move it; `entire status` shows where they go.
```

"your branch's own remote takes it over" was the earlier phrasing — hence `freshness: stale`.

To actually see the note, you need ambiguity. Either:
- add a second remote (`git remote add upstream …`), or
- give one remote two push URLs (`git remote set-url --add --push origin …`)

then run `entire doctor` (which prints it on demand) rather than re-running enable.

If you want the single-remote case to say something, that's a new behavior — the note would have to stop gating on `ambiguous()`. Worth deciding on its own rather than under this finding.

content.text:
`ambiguous()` (`remote_topology.go:145-157`) is true in either of two cases, and neither is exotic — in the ordinary repo *no* remote is pinned, since `pinned` requires a `checkpoint_remote` that's configured, owner-matched, and URL-derivable (`checkpoint/remote/util.go:212-254` — nil config → `enabled=false`).

**A. Any unpinned remote with ≥2 push URLs** (`fansOut`, `:44`):

```bash
git remote set-url --add --push origin git@github.com:you/mirror.git
```

That's the mirror-push setup — one `git push origin` delivering to two repos. Real-world: pushing to GitHub + an internal GitLab under one remote name.

**B. More than one unpinned remote** — i.e. plain "this repo has 2+ remotes":

```bash
git remote add upstream git@github.com:entireio/cli.git
```

The standard fork workflow (`origin` = your fork, `upstream` = the project) hits this, as does adding a colleague's remote to review their branch, or `git clone -o base` plus a later `origin`.

So case B is the common trigger — the note fires on any multi-remote repo, which is why the finding's single-remote scenario can't reach it. Your test repo had one remote, so both conditions were false.

To see it locally:

```bash
git remote add upstream https://example.com/x.git   # in a throwaway clone
entire doctor
```

Worth noting for the finding's second suggestion: a test pinning "silent with exactly one remote" is cheap precisely because the boundary is at two.

content.text:
Half true. The *mechanism* it describes is accurate; the *scope* it implies is not.

**What's right:** on the git-refs backend, `resolveRefsPushDestination` (`strategy/refs_push_destination.go:65-86`) does target `urls[0]` and ignore the rest when a remote has ≥2 push URLs, and `GetPushURLs` order is git's own — so the `→` marker points at the right URL. "Clone that first repository to resume elsewhere" matches the documented consequence at `:43-47`. The note also correctly gates this wording on `t.primaryIsRefs`; on the git-branch backend the fan-out is kept and the other branch of the note says so.

**What's wrong:** the note asserts this for `origin2` regardless of whether `origin2` is the elected checkpoint sync remote. Checkpoints only ride a push whose remote *is* the election — `checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote` returns false for every other remote (`checkpoint_sync_remote.go:122-141`), and that gate runs at `manual_commit_push.go:98`, before `prePushCheckpointRefs` ever resolves a destination. So in your repo, with `origin` and `origin2` and no `checkpoint_push_remote`, the election lands on `origin` (`SyncRemoteSourceDefault`) and:

- `git push origin2` carries **no** checkpoints at all — not to the first URL, not to the second.
- `https://github.com/gtrrz-victor/test-cli` (origin2's first URL) receives nothing, so "clone that first repository to resume elsewhere" sends you to a repo with no session history.

The fan-out loop in `describeCheckpointDestination` (`:167-190`) iterates every `fansOut()` remote with no reference to `t.syncRemote`, then two lines later prints the elected remote. Your output should show `origin` named just below — the note contradicts itself within four lines.

That's a second instance of the same defect class as the open finding `01M0FJ6N8PS0`: the note reads the election for one sentence and ignores it for the rest. Here the honest version is conditional — for the elected remote, "checkpoints go to the first URL only"; for any other, "this remote carries no checkpoints", which makes the URL list irrelevant.

Note the push-time warning is *not* affected: `warnIgnoredPushURLs` fires only after the gate, so it never lies. It's specifically the setup/doctor note that does.

Want me to file this as a finding on the trail?

Checkpoints sync to one remote — right now "origin". A push to a different remote of your own can move it; entire status shows where they go. And pinned for the elected remote is exactly the predicate that makes entire status print Checkpoints sync to: dedicated checkpoint remote (<repo>) — status.go:290-305 requires GetCheckpointRemote() != nil plus PushURL(elected) enabled, both implied by pinned, since PushURL returns enabled=false when the config is nil. Reachable in a mixed-ownership fork setup: checkpoint_remote set, origin = your fork (ownership matches -> pinned), upstream plus a colleague's remote (checkpointRemoteIsInherited -> unpinned). Three surfaces now read one election and only two share code; the one that opted out is the one that drifted. Routing the note through it also yields the Err string for free — the only mismatch is its CountUnpushedCheckpoints call, which the note does not need, so splitting the count off would let all three share the destination logic. I verified it against the code. **The finding is correct**, including its reachability argument.

**Confirmed mechanically**

- `describeSyncRemote` (`remote_topology.go:229-274`) never reads `pinned` — it switches only on `syncSource` and prints `t.syncRemote`. Its only caller is behind `if names := t.unpinnedNames(); len(names) > 1` (`:196`), and `unpinnedNames` (`:278-287`) excludes the pinned elected remote. So the named destination is genuinely absent from the list printed one line earlier.
- The `pinned` ⇔ status-dedicated equivalence holds. `pinned` is `remote.PushURL(name)`'s `enabled` (`:100-102`); `PushURL` returns `enabled=false` whenever `GetCheckpointRemote()` is nil (`checkpoint/remote/util.go:212-219`). Status's dedicated branch (`status.go:303-305`) requires exactly `GetCheckpointRemote() != nil` **and** `PushURL(elected)` enabled. Same predicate — so `status` prints `dedicated checkpoint remote (<repo>)` in precisely the state where the note prints `origin`.

**Reachability checks out, and it's narrower than "any checkpoint_remote repo"** — worth recording, because it's what makes the state real rather than theoretical:

- `checkpoint_remote` must be in tracked `.entire/settings.json`, not `settings.local.json`. A local-file config is "always ours" (`util.go:365-366`), so *every* remote comes back pinned → `unpinnedNames()` is empty → the note is silent. The bug needs the ownership test to split the remotes.
- With the tracked file: `origin` = your fork → origin URL and push dest both owned by the checkpoint repo's owner → not inherited → pinned. `upstream` → push dest owner mismatches → inherited → unpinned. Colleague's remote → likewise unpinned. Two unpinned → `ambiguous()` true. Exactly the setup the finding describes.

**On the root cause and the proposed fix** — I agree with routing through `computeCheckpointSyncInfo`, with one caveat the finding already spotted: it calls `countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus`, which the note doesn't want. Shape I'd use:

- extract the destination logic (`:279-322` minus the two count calls) into a helper returning `checkpointSyncInfo` with `Unpushed` unset;
- `computeCheckpointSyncInfo` = helper + the counts (status keeps its behavior byte-for-byte);
- `inspectRemoteTopology` calls the helper, dropping its own `ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` and its `syncErr` handling (the helper's `Err` replaces it);
- `describeSyncRemote` gains a `dedicated` arm and switches on the string source.

Two consequences to accept deliberately: the note becomes dependent on `settings.Load` (today it only loads the checkpoints config), and `Source` stops being the typed `strategy.CheckpointSyncRemoteSource` in the topology struct — the existing `TestDescribeSyncRemote` table would need updating to strings.

One thing the finding does *not* cover, which the same fix does not address: the fan-out block above (`:167-190`) also ignores the election, so it can claim "checkpoints go to the first URL only" for a remote that carries no checkpoints at all. That's the multi-push-URL case we looked at with your `origin2`. Separate finding, same class.

content.text:
Two different things in this code are called "pinning" — worth separating, since only one of them is the `pinned` in the finding.

**1. Pinning which *remote* carries checkpoints** (`strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`) — this is what the note's last line advises, and it makes the election `SyncRemoteSourceConfig`:

```json
// .entire/settings.local.json
{ "strategy_options": { "checkpoint_push_remote": "origin2" } }
```

Plain git remote name. Use `settings.local.json`: a remote name is per-clone, and committing it fail-closes checkpoint sync for any teammate whose clone lacks that name. Fail-closed is real here — naming a missing remote stops checkpoint sync entirely and `entire status` says so.

**2. `pinned` in `remote_topology.go`** — a *different* thing: it means `checkpoint_remote` is in effect for that remote, so checkpoints go to a dedicated store repo instead of the remote's own URLs:

```json
{ "strategy_options": { "checkpoint_remote": { "provider": "github", "repo": "gtrrz-victor/checkpoints" } } }
```

Structured object; `provider` and `repo` both required, `repo` must contain `/`, else `GetCheckpointRemote()` returns nil and nothing is pinned (`settings.go:1466-1487`).

**To reproduce the finding's state**, `pinned` has to be true for *some* remotes and false for others, which constrains where you put it:

- Put `checkpoint_remote` in tracked **`.entire/settings.json`**, not `settings.local.json`. In the local file it's "always ours" → every remote pins → `unpinnedNames()` empty → the note goes silent and you see nothing.
- Set `repo` owner = `gtrrz-victor` (matching your `origin`), so `origin` passes the ownership test and pins.
- Add two remotes owned by someone else, so they stay unpinned and `ambiguous()` trips:

```bash
git remote add upstream https://github.com/entireio/cli.git
git remote add colleague https://github.com/someone-else/test-cli.git
entire doctor
```

Expected buggy output: `This repo has 2 remotes (upstream, colleague).` followed by `Checkpoints sync to one remote — right now "origin"` — origin named but absent from the list. Then `entire status` in the same repo should say `Checkpoints sync to: dedicated checkpoint remote (gtrrz-victor/checkpoints)` — the drift.

The checkpoint repo doesn't need to exist for the note to misbehave; the ownership test is local-only, no network.

content.text:
Yes — that's the **captured election**, and it is a file in the git common dir.

```
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/entire-checkpoint-sync-remotes.json
```

```json
{"remotes":["origin2"]}
```

List-shaped on disk, but phase 1 caps it at one entry (`checkpoint_sync_capture.go:22-35, 78-91`). Writing it by hand works: the resolver just reads it and checks the name is still a configured remote (`checkpoint_sync_remote.go:93-101`). Reads are **fail-soft** — missing, unreadable, corrupt, or naming a deleted remote all fall through to the default tiers rather than disabling sync. There's a sibling lock file, `entire-checkpoint-sync-remotes.lock`, but only the CLI's read-decide-write path takes it; you don't need it for a manual edit. Note it's the *common* dir, so it's shared across worktrees.

**But that's not what the first push does unconditionally.** Capture is evidence-based and two-phase:

- The push target must agree with the branch's declared push destination — `branch.<name>.pushRemote` → `remote.pushDefault` → `branch.<name>.remote` — and differ from the current election.
- The election is persisted only *after* checkpoints actually landed there (`pendingCaptureCheckpointSyncRemote` proposes, `commitCapturedSyncRemote` writes). A push that carried nothing doesn't move it.
- **First capture sticks**: once the file has an entry, no later push replaces it.
- An explicit `checkpoint_push_remote` outranks capture and disables it entirely (setting tier comes first at `:82-89`).

So on a plain repo where you only ever push to `origin`, no capture happens at all — `origin` is already the `default` tier, so there's nothing to displace and the file never appears. You get capture when you push to a *different* remote that your branch is actually configured to push to.

Which one you want depends on what you're testing:

| goal | do this |
|---|---|
| deterministic, survives everything | `checkpoint_push_remote` in `settings.local.json` → source `config` |
| simulate a past capture | write the JSON file → source `observed` |
| exercise the real capture path | `git config branch.<b>.pushRemote origin2` then `git push origin2` |

For the `pinned` bug specifically, neither helps — `pinned` is the `checkpoint_remote` store, unrelated to these three tiers. But the capture file *is* the cheapest way to reach the `observed` arm of `describeSyncRemote`, which is otherwise only reachable through a real push.

Repo: /Users/gtrrz-victor/wks/cli/cli (Go, package `cli` at cmd/entire/cli). Design a minimal, well-argued implementation plan for one confirmed bug. Do NOT edit files — read and return a plan.

## The bug (already verified; do not re-litigate whether it is real)

`entire enable` / `entire doctor` print a "checkpoint destination" note from `cmd/entire/cli/remote_topology.go`. `describeSyncRemote` (remote_topology.go:229-274) prints `t.syncRemote` and never consults `remoteDestination.pinned`. Its only caller is gated on `if names := t.unpinnedNames(); len(names) > 1` (remote_topology.go:196-199), and `unpinnedNames` (:278-287) excludes pinned remotes. So when the ELECTED remote is pinned (a `checkpoint_remote` dedicated store is in effect for it), the note names a remote that is (a) missing from the remote list it just printed and (b) not where checkpoints land — they land in the dedicated store repo.

`pinned` is set at remote_topology.go:100-102 from `checkpointremote.PushURL(ctx, name)`'s `enabled` return. `entire status` uses the SAME predicate for its dedicated branch (status.go:303-305: `s.GetCheckpointRemote() != nil` && `PushURL(elected)` enabled) and prints `Checkpoints sync to: dedicated checkpoint remote (<org/repo>)`. So status and enable/doctor disagree in exactly this state.

Reachability (verified): `checkpoint_remote` must be in TRACKED `.entire/settings.json` (in `settings.local.json` every remote pins, so `unpinnedNames()` is empty and the note is silent); origin = the user's own fork so ownership matches and origin pins; `upstream` + a colleague remote fail `checkpointRemoteIsInherited` and stay unpinned → `ambiguous()` true.

## The proposed root-cause fix (evaluate and detail it; propose something better only if you find a concrete problem with it)

`inspectRemoteTopology` (remote_topology.go:115) calls `strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` directly, bypassing `computeCheckpointSyncInfo` (status.go:279-322), which status.go:258-261 documents as "the single shared computation behind both the text and JSON checkpoint-sync sections … so the two outputs cannot drift" and which already handles dedicated mode. Three surfaces read one election; the one that opted out drifted.

Plan the extraction: split the destination logic out of `computeCheckpointSyncInfo` into a helper that returns `checkpointSyncInfo` WITHOUT the unpushed count (the note does not need it and must stay cheap/offline), have `computeCheckpointSyncInfo` = helper + counts so `entire status` behaviour is byte-for-byte unchanged (note its dedicated branch conditions the count on `checkpoint.PrimaryIsRefs`), and have `inspectRemoteTopology` use the helper.

Both files are package `cli`, same package — no import cycle.

## Specific things your plan must resolve

1. The topology struct today has `syncRemote string`, `syncSource strategy.CheckpointSyncRemoteSource`, `syncErr error` (remote_topology.go:53-68). If it instead stores a `checkpointSyncInfo`, `Source` becomes a plain string and `Err` a string. Say exactly what the struct becomes and what `describeSyncRemote`'s switch compares against. Check whether `.golangci.yaml` enables `exhaustive` or any switch linter that reacts to this.
2. What `settings` value the helper needs (`*EntireSettings`), where `inspectRemoteTopology` gets it, and what happens when that load FAILS. Note `ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` itself fail-closes on a settings read error, and the note renders `Err` as "Checkpoints are NOT syncing: …". Keep the note best-effort — it must never obstruct enable/doctor.
3. Exact new wording for the dedicated arm of `describeSyncRemote`, at the note's 4-space indent, matching the surrounding voice (read the existing arms and their doc comment at :207-228). Facts it must convey: checkpoints go to the dedicated store `<org/repo>` configured by `checkpoint_remote`, NOT to any of the remotes listed above it. Consider that the note's closing advice line (:191-193) tells the user to "set checkpoint_remote" — which is already done in this state, so decide whether that line needs suppressing in dedicated mode.
4. Test plan. Existing: `TestDescribeSyncRemote` in cmd/entire/cli/remote_topology_test.go builds `remoteTopology` literals and calls `describeSyncRemote` directly (so a struct change edits every case). No test currently reaches `describeCheckpointDestination` at all. Propose (a) a dedicated-arm case, (b) a table test over `describeCheckpointDestination` covering the buggy scenario (destinations colleague/origin-pinned/upstream, elected origin, dedicated) plus the single-remote silent case, and (c) whether the extraction needs a status-side test. Prefer table tests with `t.Parallel()`, matching the existing file's style.
5. Call out anything in `entire status` output that must NOT change, and how the implementer verifies that.

Return: ordered steps with file:line anchors, the exact struct/function signatures you propose, the proposed user-visible strings, and the test list. Be concise and concrete; flag any risk you find with the approach.

### Why this shape

`/Users/gtrrz-victor/wks/cli/cli/cmd/entire/cli/status.go:258-261` already declares `checkpointSyncInfo` the single shared computation "so the two outputs cannot drift", and it is the only place that knows about dedicated mode (`checkpointSyncSourceDedicated`, status.go:256). `inspectRemoteTopology` (remote_topology.go:115) calls `strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` directly, i.e. it opted out of that contract, and drifted exactly where the contract would have covered it. Extraction is the minimal fix that also closes the class.

---

### Step 1 — extract the destination-only helper (status.go:279-322)

New function, placed immediately above `computeCheckpointSyncInfo`:

```go
// resolveCheckpointSyncDestination answers only *where* checkpoints go — the
// elected remote, the dedicated store, or the fail-closed error — with no
// unpushed count. Split out so surfaces that only need the destination
// (remoteTopology's note) share this one election instead of re-deriving it.
// Local-only and cheap: no ref walks, no push-queue read, no network.
// s may be nil when the caller could not load settings; dedicated mode is then
// simply not detected, matching the best-effort contract of those callers.
func resolveCheckpointSyncDestination(ctx context.Context, s *EntireSettings) checkpointSyncInfo
```

Body = status.go:280-306 verbatim, with two edits:
- the `if cr := s.GetCheckpointRemote()` guard becomes `if s != nil { if cr := ...` (nil receiver would panic in `settings.go:1467` on `s.StrategyOptions`),
- the dedicated arm returns `checkpointSyncInfo{Remote: cr.Repo, Source: checkpointSyncSourceDedicated}` with **no** `LoadCheckpointsConfig`/`countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus` block, and the tail returns `{Remote: elected.Name, Source: string(elected.Source)}` with no count.

`computeCheckpointSyncInfo` keeps its signature and becomes helper + counts:

```go
func computeCheckpointSyncInfo(ctx context.Context, s *EntireSettings) checkpointSyncInfo {
	info := resolveCheckpointSyncDestination(ctx, s)
	switch {
	case info.Err != "" || info.Remote == "":
		return info
	case info.Source == checkpointSyncSourceDedicated:
		// Counting comment from status.go:310-313 moves here verbatim.
		if cpCfg, cfgErr := settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig(ctx); cfgErr == nil && checkpoint.PrimaryIsRefs(cpCfg) {
			info.Unpushed = countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus(ctx, "")
		}
	default:
		info.Unpushed = countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus(ctx, info.Remote)
	}
	return info
}
```

This is order-preserving and condition-preserving (the `PrimaryIsRefs` gate stays only on the dedicated arm), so `entire status` is byte-for-byte unchanged. Keep the two long "Accepted divergence" comments with the code they describe (the PushURL probe comment goes to the helper, the fail-closed one to the helper's error return).

### Step 2 — restructure `remoteTopology` (remote_topology.go:48-70)

Replace the three fields at :55-69 with one:

```go
// sync is the shared checkpoint-destination computation (status.go), so this
// note, `entire status` text and `entire status --json` cannot disagree about
// where checkpoints land. Its Unpushed is always 0 here: the note only needs
// the destination and must stay offline and cheap.
sync checkpointSyncInfo
```

Keep the existing prose about why an empty name names nothing and why a fail-closed election must still speak — fold it into this comment; it now describes `sync.Remote == ""` and `sync.Err != ""`.

In `inspectRemoteTopology` (remote_topology.go:112-122):

```go
// Best-effort: on a settings read failure the note simply cannot tell whether
// a dedicated checkpoint_remote is in effect, so it falls back to whatever the
// resolver says. Never surface the load error — the note renders Err as
// "Checkpoints are NOT syncing", which a transient read failure is not.
s, err := LoadEntireSettings(ctx)          // config.go:33
if err != nil {
	logging.Debug(ctx, "remote topology: could not load settings", slog.String("error", err.Error()))
	s = nil
}
t.sync = resolveCheckpointSyncDestination(ctx, s)
```

`strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` is no longer called from this file; the `strategy` import stays (used by the switch). The `logging`/`slog` imports stay.

### Step 3 — `describeSyncRemote` (remote_topology.go:229-274)

Guards become `if t.sync.Remote == ""` / `if t.sync.Err != ""` (`Fprintf(..., "    Checkpoints are NOT syncing: %s\n", t.sync.Err)` — `%s`, not `%v`, now that it is a string; `perfsprint`/`govet` are fine either way but `%s` is right).

The switch becomes `switch t.sync.Source` comparing **string forms**, matching the precedent already in `writeCheckpointSyncLines` (status.go:352-357):

```go
case string(strategy.SyncRemoteSourceConfig):
case string(strategy.SyncRemoteSourceObserved):
case string(strategy.SyncRemoteSourceDefault), string(strategy.SyncRemoteSourceSole), string(strategy.SyncRemoteSourceFirst):
case checkpointSyncSourceDedicated:   // new

```
```
    Checkpoints go to the dedicated store "org/checkpoints" (set by

```

Deliberately omits "a push to any other remote carries your code but no session history": in dedicated mode checkpoints never ride a code push at all, so that sentence would mislead. For context on where I've landed since asking — the design pass came back and settled most of the mechanics, so the two open points are narrower than I framed them:

**Q1 (scope)** is just: does this change fix only the dedicated/pinned drift the finding describes, or also the fan-out block at `remote_topology.go:175-195`, which says "checkpoints go to the first URL only" for a multi-push-URL remote without checking whether that remote is the elected one — your `origin2` case. Same class of defect, but a second objective in one PR.

**Q2 (typed source)** is a genuine tradeoff I can't resolve from the code alone. Sharing status.go's computation means `Source` arrives as a plain `string`, so the note's `switch` stops being checked by the `exhaustive` linter — and this repo leans on that deliberately (`checkpoint_sync_capture.go:160-163`: "Enumerated rather than left to a default so `exhaustive` turns a new tier into a decision here"). Three ways out: introduce a named source type so both switches stay checked; accept the string and add a `default:` arm that degrades to a true sentence; or don't share at all and teach `remote_topology.go` about `pinned` itself. The design pass recommends the middle one, noting status.go already lives with it.

Everything else is decided: extract a `resolveCheckpointSyncDestination` helper (destination only, no unpushed count), leave `computeCheckpointSyncInfo` as helper + counts so `entire status` output is byte-for-byte unchanged, add a dedicated arm to `describeSyncRemote`, suppress the closing "set checkpoint_remote" advice when that's already what's configured, and add the first test coverage `describeCheckpointDestination` has ever had.

content.text:
Let me lay out the whole state space first, then we can decide row by row. The note has three claim-making parts — the fan-out block (`:175-195`), the remote list (`:196-197`), and the sync line (`:198`) — and each one can be true or false independently.

## Every scenario

| # | Setup | Today | Correct? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | no remotes | silent | ✓ |
| 2 | 1 remote, 1 push URL | silent | ✓ |
| 3 | 1 remote, 2 push URLs | fan-out block only | ✓ — that remote is necessarily the elected one |
| 4 | 2+ remotes, no fan-out, no dedicated | list + "right now *origin*" | ✓ |
| 5 | 2+ remotes, fan-out **on the elected remote** | block + list + sync line | ✓ (odd order — the URL detail lands before the destination) |
| 6 | 2+ remotes, fan-out on a **non-elected** remote | "checkpoints go to the first URL only" | ✗ that remote carries **no** checkpoints — your `origin2` case |
| 7 | dedicated in effect for the elected remote (tracked `settings.json`, mixed ownership) | names `origin`, which is absent from the list | ✗ the finding |
| 8 | dedicated in `settings.local.json` (every remote pins) | silent | ✓-ish — destination is the store and *any* push delivers, so nothing is ambiguous |
| 9 | `checkpoint_remote` present but not in effect for the elected remote | normal elected-remote wording | ✓ |
| 10 | fail-closed election (`checkpoint_push_remote` names a missing remote) | "NOT syncing" — **but** a fan-out block above it may still claim URLs receive checkpoints | ✗ third instance |
| 11 | election unreadable (transient git failure) | generic fallback sentence, same fan-out caveat | ✗ same |

So it's one defect repeated: **the fan-out block and the remote list never consult the election, and the sync line never consults `pinned`.** Rows 6, 7, 10, 11 are all that.

## The principle I'd apply

Every claim gets conditioned on the election, and the note is ordered destination-first:

```
Checkpoint destination: REVIEW
  This repo has 3 remotes (colleague, origin, upstream).
  Checkpoints sync to one remote — right now "origin". A push to a different
  remote of your own can move it; `entire status` shows where they go.
  Remote "origin" pushes to 2 URLs:
    → https://github.com/you/app
      https://github.com/you/mirror
    Checkpoints go to the first URL only; the others receive your code but
    no session history.
```

and in dedicated mode:

```
  This repo has 3 remotes (colleague, origin, upstream).
  Checkpoints go to the dedicated store "org/checkpoints" (set by
  checkpoint_remote), not to any of these remotes. Your pushes to "origin"
  carry them there.
```

That last clause matters in row 7: pushing only to `upstream` strands the transcripts, and nothing else in the output tells you that.

Three decisions I can't make for you:

Verified — and it simplifies the design.

`hasCheckpointURL` (the pre-push exemption) is set from exactly `PushURL(pushRemote).enabled` (`checkpoint_remote.go:92-102`), which is the same predicate as `pinned`. So **pinned remotes are precisely the ones whose pushes deliver to the store** — the carrier clause should name the pinned remotes, not the elected one (identical output in your scenario, since `pinned = {origin} = elected`, but correct in general).

And the fan-out conditioning needs no new plumbing: a pinned remote's `fansOut()` is already false, so in dedicated mode every fanning-out remote is by definition not carrying checkpoints. `d.name == t.sync.Remote` covers rows 6, 10 and 11 in one condition, and the shared `checkpointSyncInfo` needs no new field.

# Make the checkpoint-destination note consult the election on every claim

## Context

`entire enable` and `entire doctor` print a "checkpoint destination" note
(`cmd/entire/cli/remote_topology.go`) when the repo's remotes make it non-obvious
where checkpoints land. The note makes three independent claims — a per-remote
push-URL breakdown, a remote list, and a sync-destination line — and **none of
them consults the election** except the last, which consults it but ignores
`pinned`.

Trail #1108 finding `01M0FJ6N8PS0` reports one instance: when the elected remote
is pinned by a `checkpoint_remote` store, the note names a remote that is absent
from the list it just printed and is not where checkpoints go, while `entire
status` names the store — the two surfaces disagree in exactly this state.
Reviewing the whole state space found the same defect three more times.

| # | Setup | Today | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-5, 8, 9 | no remotes / 1 remote / fan-out on the elected remote / 2+ remotes / dedicated in `settings.local.json` / `checkpoint_remote` not in effect | correct | ✓ |
| 6 | fan-out on a **non-elected** remote | "checkpoints go to the first URL only" — it carries none | ✗ |
| 7 | dedicated store in effect for the elected remote | names the pinned remote, not the store | ✗ (the finding) |
| 10 | fail-closed election | "NOT syncing", but a URL block above still claims delivery | ✗ |
| 11 | election unreadable | same | ✗ |

Outcome: every claim in the note is conditioned on the election, and the note
reads destination-first.

## Design decisions (agreed)

1. **Fan-out block prints only for the elected remote.** Non-elected fanning-out
   remotes get no URL claim; a failed or unreadable election suppresses it
   entirely.
2. **Dedicated mode names the store and the carrier.** Pinned remotes are exactly
   the ones whose pushes reach the store — `hasCheckpointURL` (`strategy/checkpoint_remote.go:92-102`)
   is set from the same `PushURL(...).enabled` that sets `pinned`
   (`remote_topology.go:100-102`) — so the carrier clause names `pinnedNames()`.
3. **The remote list counts every remote**, so the elected one can never vanish
   from it. The note's gate (`ambiguous()`) is unchanged, so row 8 stays silent.

## Steps

### 1. Extract a destination-only helper — `cmd/entire/cli/status.go:279-322`

`computeCheckpointSyncInfo` is documented at `status.go:258-261` as "the single
shared computation … so the two outputs cannot drift". Split the destination
half out so a third surface can share it without paying for the counts:

```go
// resolveCheckpointSyncDestination answers only *where* checkpoints go, with no
// unpushed count: local-only, no ref walk, no push-queue read. s may be nil when
// the caller could not load settings; dedicated mode is then simply not detected.
func resolveCheckpointSyncDestination(ctx context.Context, s *EntireSettings) checkpointSyncInfo
```

Body = `status.go:280-306` verbatim, minus both count calls, with the
`s.GetCheckpointRemote()` access nil-guarded. `computeCheckpointSyncInfo` keeps
its signature and becomes helper + counts, preserving the `PrimaryIsRefs` gate on
the dedicated arm only:

```go
info := resolveCheckpointSyncDestination(ctx, s)
switch {
case info.Err != "" || info.Remote == "":
    return info
case info.Source == checkpointSyncSourceDedicated:
    if cpCfg, err := settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig(ctx); err == nil && checkpoint.PrimaryIsRefs(cpCfg) {
        info.Unpushed = countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus(ctx, "")
    }
default:
    info.Unpushed = countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus(ctx, info.Remote)
}
return info
```

Keep each "Accepted divergence" comment with the code it describes. Add
`func (i checkpointSyncInfo) dedicated() bool` next to the struct — both surfaces
need it.

**No new field is needed.** In non-dedicated mode `Remote` is the elected remote
name; in dedicated mode every fanning-out remote is unpinned and therefore not
the carrier, so the fan-out conditioning never needs the elected name there.

### 2. Store the shared result — `remote_topology.go:53-68`, `:112-122`

Replace `syncRemote` / `syncSource` / `syncErr` with one field:

```go
// sync is the shared checkpoint-destination computation (status.go), so this
// note, `entire status` and `entire status --json` cannot disagree. Unpushed is
// always 0 here: the note needs the destination only, and must stay cheap.
sync checkpointSyncInfo
```

Fold the existing prose about "an empty name names nothing" and "a fail-closed
election must still speak" into that comment. In `inspectRemoteTopology`, drop
the `strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` call and use `LoadEntireSettings`
(`config.go:33`), degrading to `s = nil` with a debug log on error — never
synthesize an `Err`, which would print "NOT syncing" for a transient read failure.

Add `pinnedNames()` beside `unpinnedNames()` (`:277-287`).

### 3. Reorder and condition the note — `remote_topology.go:160-204`

New order, destination first:

```
header
[if len(unpinnedNames()) > 1]  "This repo has N remotes (<every remote>)."   // all names now
[sync line]                    dedicated | elected | NOT syncing | unknown
[fan-out block]                only for the remote whose name == t.sync.Remote, and not dedicated
[advice line]                  suppressed when dedicated or Err
```

The fan-out loop condition becomes `d.fansOut() && !t.dedicated() && d.name == t.sync.Remote`
— one condition covering rows 6, 10 and 11, since an empty `Remote` matches
nothing. The advice line (`:191-193`) tells the user to set `checkpoint_remote`,
which is already done in dedicated mode and off-target on a fail-closed election.

### 4. Dedicated arm of `describeSyncRemote` — `remote_topology.go:229-274`

Handle dedicated with an early return **before** the switch, then convert back to
the enum for the switch tag:

```go
if t.sync.dedicated() { /* wording below */ return }
switch strategy.CheckpointSyncRemoteSource(t.sync.Source) { /* existing arms */ }
```

This keeps `exhaustive` (enabled in `.golangci.yaml`, and deliberately relied on —
see `strategy/checkpoint_sync_capture.go:160-163`) enforcing the tier switch,
which a plain-string switch would silently lose.

Wording, at the note's 4-space indent:

```
    Checkpoints go to the dedicated store "org/checkpoints" (set by
    checkpoint_remote), not to any of these remotes. Pushes to "origin"
    carry them there.
```

Last sentence lists `pinnedNames()`. It deliberately omits "a push to any other
remote carries your code but no session history" — in dedicated mode checkpoints
never ride a code push at all. Extend the doc comment at `:207-228` with the
reason.

### 5. Tests — `remote_topology_test.go` (88 lines, one test today)

`TestDescribeSyncRemote`'s six literals become `remoteTopology{sync: checkpointSyncInfo{...}}`.
Add a dedicated case. Then two new tests:

- **`TestDescribeCheckpointDestination`** (table, `t.Parallel()`) — first coverage
  of that function:
  - single remote → empty output; all-pinned (row 8) → empty output
  - **row 7**: `colleague`/`origin`(pinned)/`upstream`, dedicated store. Want the
    3-remote list, the store slug, `Pushes to "origin"`; **absent** `right now`,
    `To pin one repository`
  - **row 6**: `origin` elected, `origin2` fans out → absent `pushes to 2 URLs`
  - **row 5**: elected remote fans out → present, `→` marker on URL 0
  - **row 10**: `Err` set + a fanning-out remote → `NOT syncing`, no URL block
- **`TestInspectRemoteTopology_DedicatedStore`** — a real temp repo via
  `setupTestRepo` / `writeSettings` / `testutil.AddRemote` (pattern at
  `status_test.go:2248-2273`), tracked `settings.json` with
  `{"provider":"github","repo":"org/checkpoints"}`, `origin` = `github.com/org/repo`
  (owner match → pinned), plus two foreign remotes. Asserts the real end-to-end
  note. This is the test that would have caught the finding; the literal tables
  cannot, because they hand-build the state the bug is about.

No new status-side test: the eight `TestRunStatus_CheckpointSync*` tests
(`status_test.go:2084-2311`) verify the extraction by passing unchanged.

## Verification

```bash
go test ./cmd/entire/cli -run 'TestRunStatus_CheckpointSync|TestRunStatusJSON_CheckpointSync|TestDescribeSyncRemote|TestDescribeCheckpointDestination|TestInspectRemoteTopology'
go test -tags integration ./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test -run CheckpointSyncRemote
mise run fmt && mise run lint    # lint after fmt; see the repo's lint-binary caveat
mise run check
```

`entire status` output must not change — capture it before and after on a repo
with a dedicated store and diff. Manual end-to-end for the note:

```bash
# row 7
git remote add upstream https://github.com/entireio/cli.git
git remote add colleague https://github.com/someone/test-cli.git
# .entire/settings.json (tracked): strategy_options.checkpoint_remote = {provider, repo: <you>/checkpoints}
entire doctor      # store named, origin listed, no "right now \"origin\""
entire status      # must still say: dedicated checkpoint remote (<you>/checkpoints)

# row 6
git remote set-url --add --push origin2 https://github.com/you/test-cli2
entire doctor      # no URL block for origin2 while origin is elected
```

## Out of scope

`entire status` behaviour, the `ambiguous()` gate, and the dismissed finding
`01M0F4K9Y8WR` (the `SyncRemoteSourceSole` wording), which stays unreachable —
the new single-remote test case pins that.

1. TRIGGER — checkpoints are pushed ONLY from the git pre-push hook, during the user's own `git push` (ManualCommitStrategy.prePush, strategy/manual_commit_push.go:50). Nothing pushes at commit time or session end. push_sessions:false disables it entirely.

2. TWO DIFFERENT KNOBS, easy to conflate in user-facing text:
   - checkpoint_push_remote = a remote NAME. Elects which remote's pushes carry checkpoints. Checkpoints land in THAT remote's repo (entire/checkpoints/v1 on git-branch, refs/entire/* on git-refs).
   - checkpoint_remote = a dedicated repo (provider+repo), resolved to a URL. A separate checkpoint store.
   When checkpoint_remote is in effect it WINS and makes checkpoint_push_remote irrelevant to the destination: the single-remote gate is skipped entirely (manual_commit_push.go:78-101), so ANY push — origin or upstream — attempts delivery to that separate repo.

3. checkpoint_push_remote = "remote2" behaviour:
   - push to remote2 → carries checkpoints. push to remote1 → code only, gate returns before any checkpoint push (checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote, strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote.go:122). Push to a raw URL → also gated out (git hands the hook the URL, never the elected name).
   - Top precedence tier and FAIL-CLOSED: if the named remote does not exist, checkpoint sync is disabled everywhere until fixed — not a fallback to origin.
   - No capture can displace it, and the gated push is SILENT by design: hintGatedCheckpointSync returns early when the election source is Config (checkpoint_sync_remote.go:163), only a debug log. Worth considering for wording: with config-pinned election the user gets no push-time feedback at all, so status/doctor is the only place they learn a push to remote1 dropped checkpoints.
   - ASYMMETRY worth surfacing: reads are NOT restricted the same way. origin stays a read-only legacy tier, so resume/explain/discovery consult the elected remote first then still try origin (CheckpointReadRemotes).

4. Election tiers (ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote, checkpoint_sync_remote.go:74): checkpoint_push_remote (fail-closed) → captured/observed (fail-soft) → origin → sole remote → first in .git/config order.

5. checkpoint_remote is RE-DECIDED PER PUSH and can silently switch off (remote.PushURL, checkpoint/remote/util.go:194 → checkpointRemoteIsInherited, util.go:405):
   - Declared in .entire/settings.local.json → per-clone, always yours, NO ownership check (settings.CheckpointRemoteIsLocalOnly).
   - Declared in committed .entire/settings.json → origin's URL owner AND EVERY push URL of the remote being pushed must match the checkpoint repo's owner. With 2 push URLs that is 2 separate identities; one mismatch or unparseable owner ⇒ treated as inherited ⇒ warning logged, checkpoint_remote ignored, target falls back to the push remote, and the sync gate applies again.
   - So `git push origin` is checked against origin's url + origin's 2 push URLs; `git push upstream` against origin's url + upstream's 2 push URLs. Usual outcome for a real upstream: checkpoint_remote dropped for that push, gate kicks in, checkpoints stay local with the "N checkpoint(s) are waiting to sync to …" stderr hint. This is a good candidate for an explicit doctor line — today it is only a log warning.

6. DESTINATION SHAPE:
   - checkpoint_remote in effect → ONE URL; git's multi-push-URL fan-out is bypassed because the target is a URL not a name (refs_push_destination.go:70). The remote's 2nd push URL never receives checkpoints.
   - Transport (SSH vs HTTPS) derives from the FIRST push URL of the remote being pushed. ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN forces HTTPS. Unmappable protocol (file://, entire://) routes to the provider's canonical host over HTTPS rather than misrouting to origin.
   - Falling back to a remote NAME with 2 push URLs: git-branch pushes v1 to BOTH; git-refs pushes to the FIRST ONLY and warns ("Checkpoints go to one repository: … N other push URL(s) … will not receive them", refs_push_destination.go:110).
   - Trails always go to the user's push remote, never the checkpoint repo. The empty-remote publication deferral (deferCheckpointPushOnEmptyRemote) does not apply when checkpoint_remote is in effect.
   - git-branch only: one-time bootstrap fetch of the metadata branch (fetchMetadataBranchIfMissing); skipped on git-refs.

7. OPF, if enabled, re-redacts unpushed v1 commits before the push and can abort it.

Existing user-facing surfaces you are presumably rewording: strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote.go hintGatedCheckpointSync, strategy/refs_push_destination.go warnIgnoredPushURLs, cli/remote_topology.go describeCheckpointDestination/describeSyncRemote (shared by enable and doctor), and entire status's destination + unpushed count.

Two gaps that stood out while reading, if you want message-level coverage for them: (a) the config-pinned election producing a completely silent gated push, and (b) the per-push inheritance rejection of checkpoint_remote being log-only.

content.text:
A peer session (cli-19) traced the push routing independently and sent its findings. Most of it confirms the model this plan is built on; two things are worth acting on.

**Confirmed** — pinned-per-remote is the right predicate (their point 5: ownership is checked against origin's URL *and* every push URL of the remote being pushed, which is exactly what `remote.PushURL` does), and dedicated mode bypasses git's fan-out because the target is a URL not a name (their 6, `refs_push_destination.go:70`). That's the basis for suppressing the URL block in dedicated mode.

**One correction to their summary:** their point 2 says that with `checkpoint_remote` in effect, "ANY push — origin or upstream — attempts delivery to that separate repo". That's only true for a `settings.local.json` declaration, which skips the ownership check. For a committed `settings.json` — the case our finding needs — the check runs per push remote, so `upstream` typically falls back and the gate applies. Their own point 5 says this precisely; point 2 is the loose version. Our plan follows point 5.

**Two gaps they flagged**, against my scenario matrix:

- **(a) config-pinned election gives a silent gated push** — `hintGatedCheckpointSync` returns early when the source is `config`, so pushing to the wrong remote says nothing at push time. Already covered by the note's existing `config` arm ("A push to any other remote carries your code but no session history"), which is arguably the right place for it. No change needed.
- **(b) the per-push inheritance rejection is log-only** — this is my row 9. When `checkpoint_remote` is configured but rejected as inherited, `remote.PushURL` logs a warning (`checkpoint/remote/util.go:249`) and nothing user-facing ever mentions it. `entire status` shows the elected remote as though no store were configured (pinned by `TestRunStatus_CheckpointSyncDedicated_IneligibleFallsBackToElected`). My plan marks row 9 "correct" because every claim it makes is true — but it's silently ignoring a setting the user wrote.

That last one is a real gap and cheap to cover here (`HasCheckpointRemoteKey()` plus the per-remote `pinned` we already compute), but it's a second objective.

To restate the question plainly, in case the framing was the problem: someone sets `checkpoint_remote` in the committed `.entire/settings.json`, pointing at their own checkpoint store. The question is whether this change should also surface that, or leave it for a separate one. Three angles I can expand on if any of them is the sticking point:

- **Is it actually a problem?** For the teammate the current behaviour is right and arguably needs no comment. For the *author* of the setting it's a misconfiguration they'd want to know about — and the note can't tell the two apart.
- **Where it would appear.** The note only prints on ambiguous repos, so it wouldn't fire on the common single-remote clone. `doctor`-only is the quieter option.

# Make the checkpoint-destination note consult the election on every claim

## Context

`entire enable` and `entire doctor` print a "checkpoint destination" note
(`cmd/entire/cli/remote_topology.go`) when the repo's remotes make it non-obvious
where checkpoints land. The note makes three independent claims — a per-remote
push-URL breakdown, a remote list, and a sync-destination line — and **none of
them consults the election** except the last, which consults it but ignores
`pinned`.

Trail #1108 finding `01M0FJ6N8PS0` reports one instance: when the elected remote
is pinned by a `checkpoint_remote` store, the note names a remote that is absent
from the list it just printed and is not where checkpoints go, while `entire
status` names the store — the two surfaces disagree in exactly this state.
Reviewing the whole state space found the same defect three more times, plus one
state nothing reports at all.

| # | Setup | Today | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-5, 8 | no remotes / 1 remote / fan-out on the elected remote / 2+ remotes / dedicated in `settings.local.json` | correct | ✓ |
| 6 | fan-out on a **non-elected** remote | "checkpoints go to the first URL only" — it carries none | ✗ |
| 7 | dedicated store in effect for the elected remote | names the pinned remote, not the store | ✗ (the finding) |
| 9 | `checkpoint_remote` configured but rejected for the elected remote | nothing — a `logging.Warn` only | ✗ silent |
| 10 | fail-closed election | "NOT syncing", but a URL block above still claims delivery | ✗ |
| 11 | election unreadable | same | ✗ |

Outcome: every claim in the note is conditioned on the election, and a
`checkpoint_remote` that is being ignored is said out loud.

## Design decisions (agreed)

1. **Fan-out block prints only for the elected remote.** Non-elected fanning-out
   remotes get no URL claim; a failed or unreadable election suppresses it
   entirely.
2. **Dedicated mode names the store and the carrier.** Pinned remotes are exactly
   the ones whose pushes reach the store — `hasCheckpointURL`
   (`strategy/checkpoint_remote.go:92-102`) is set from the same
   `PushURL(...).enabled` that sets `pinned` (`remote_topology.go:100-102`) — so
   the carrier clause names `pinnedNames()`.
3. **The remote list counts every remote**, so the elected one can never vanish
   from it. The note's gate (`ambiguous()`) is unchanged, so row 8 stays silent.
4. **Row 9 is reported in `status` and in the note.** Checkpoints still sync in
   that state — they go to the elected remote — so the wording must say the
   *setting* is not in effect, never that checkpoints are lost. The cause cannot
   be asserted: `enabled=false` covers the ownership rejection, an unparseable
   push URL, and an unmappable protocol (`checkpoint/remote/util.go:244-300`),
   and `PushURL` does not return which. Name the common cause as a likelihood.

## Steps

### 1. Extract a destination-only helper — `cmd/entire/cli/status.go:279-322`

`computeCheckpointSyncInfo` is documented at `status.go:258-261` as "the single
shared computation … so the two outputs cannot drift". Split the destination
half out so a third surface can share it without paying for the counts:

```go
// resolveCheckpointSyncDestination answers only *where* checkpoints go, with no
// unpushed count: local-only, no ref walk, no push-queue read. s may be nil when
// the caller could not load settings; dedicated mode is then simply not detected.
func resolveCheckpointSyncDestination(ctx context.Context, s *EntireSettings) checkpointSyncInfo
```

Body = `status.go:280-306` verbatim, minus both count calls, with the
`s.GetCheckpointRemote()` access nil-guarded. `computeCheckpointSyncInfo` keeps
its signature and becomes helper + counts, preserving the `PrimaryIsRefs` gate on
the dedicated arm only:

```go
info := resolveCheckpointSyncDestination(ctx, s)
switch {
case info.Err != "" || info.Remote == "":
    return info
case info.Source == checkpointSyncSourceDedicated:
    if cpCfg, err := settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig(ctx); err == nil && checkpoint.PrimaryIsRefs(cpCfg) {
        info.Unpushed = countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus(ctx, "")
    }
default:
    info.Unpushed = countUnpushedCheckpointsForStatus(ctx, info.Remote)
}
return info
```

Keep each "Accepted divergence" comment with the code it describes. Add
`func (i checkpointSyncInfo) dedicated() bool` next to the struct — both surfaces
need it.

**No new field is needed for the note's own claims.** In non-dedicated mode
`Remote` is the elected remote name; in dedicated mode every fanning-out remote
is unpinned and therefore not the carrier, so the fan-out conditioning never
needs the elected name there.

### 2. Row 9: carry the ignored store in the shared struct — `status.go:262-277`

```go
// IgnoredStore names a checkpoint_remote that is configured but NOT in effect
// for the elected remote, so checkpoints fall back to that remote. Empty in
// every other state, including dedicated mode (where it IS in effect).
IgnoredStore string
```

Set in the helper when `s.GetCheckpointRemote() != nil` and the dedicated branch
was not taken. Malformed `checkpoint_remote` entries (`HasCheckpointRemoteKey()`
true, `GetCheckpointRemote()` nil) are out of scope — a separate silent-ignore
worth its own finding.

### 3. Report row 9 in `entire status` — `status.go:340-365`, `:751-754`, `:818-822`

After the destination line, when `info.IgnoredStore != ""`:

```
  ! checkpoint_remote "org/checkpoints" is not in effect; checkpoints go to origin
```

Rendered with `sty.yellow`, matching the existing `! Checkpoints NOT syncing:`
convention. JSON gains `checkpoint_remote_ignored` (omitempty) next to
`checkpoint_sync_remote` at `status.go:751`, so the state is reachable
non-interactively.

### 4. Store the shared result in the topology — `remote_topology.go:53-68`, `:112-122`

Replace `syncRemote` / `syncSource` / `syncErr` with one field:

```go
// sync is the shared checkpoint-destination computation (status.go), so this
// note, `entire status` and `entire status --json` cannot disagree. Unpushed is
// always 0 here: the note needs the destination only, and must stay cheap.
sync checkpointSyncInfo
```

Fold the existing prose about "an empty name names nothing" and "a fail-closed
election must still speak" into that comment. In `inspectRemoteTopology`, drop
the `strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` call and use `LoadEntireSettings`
(`config.go:33`), degrading to `s = nil` with a debug log on error — never
synthesize an `Err`, which would print "NOT syncing" for a transient read failure.

Add `pinnedNames()` beside `unpinnedNames()` (`:277-287`).

### 5. Reorder and condition the note — `remote_topology.go:160-204`

New order, destination first:

```
header
[if len(unpinnedNames()) > 1]  "This repo has N remotes (<every remote>)."   // all names now
[sync line]                    dedicated | elected | NOT syncing | unknown
[if IgnoredStore != ""]        the row-9 line (below)
[fan-out block]                only for the remote whose name == t.sync.Remote, and not dedicated
[advice line]                  suppressed when dedicated, Err, or IgnoredStore
```

The fan-out loop condition becomes `d.fansOut() && !t.dedicated() && d.name == t.sync.Remote`
— one condition covering rows 6, 10 and 11, since an empty `Remote` matches
nothing. The advice line (`:191-193`) tells the user to set `checkpoint_remote`,
which is already done in rows 7 and 9 and off-target on a fail-closed election.

Row-9 wording, at the note's 4-space indent:

```
    A checkpoint_remote ("org/checkpoints") is configured but not in effect
    here — most often because it looks like it belongs to another owner.
    Checkpoints go to "origin" instead; set it in .entire/settings.local.json
    if the store is yours.
```

The last clause is the actual fix: a local-file declaration skips the ownership
check (`settings.CheckpointRemoteIsLocalOnly`, `checkpoint/remote/util.go:412`).
Note the consequence: `enable` shares this note with `doctor`, so a fresh fork
clone sees the line on first enable. That reads as useful rather than noisy — it
is the moment the inherited setting first fails — but it is a deliberate choice.

### 6. Dedicated arm of `describeSyncRemote` — `remote_topology.go:229-274`

Handle dedicated with an early return **before** the switch, then convert back to
the enum for the switch tag:

```go
if t.sync.dedicated() { /* wording below */ return }
switch strategy.CheckpointSyncRemoteSource(t.sync.Source) { /* existing arms */ }
```

This keeps `exhaustive` (enabled in `.golangci.yaml`, and deliberately relied on —
see `strategy/checkpoint_sync_capture.go:160-163`) enforcing the tier switch,
which a plain-string switch would silently lose.

Wording:

```
    Checkpoints go to the dedicated store "org/checkpoints" (set by
    checkpoint_remote), not to any of these remotes. Pushes to "origin"
    carry them there.
```

Last sentence lists `pinnedNames()`. It deliberately omits "a push to any other
remote carries your code but no session history" — in dedicated mode checkpoints
never ride a code push at all. Extend the doc comment at `:207-228` with the
reason.

### 7. Tests

`remote_topology_test.go` (88 lines, one test today). `TestDescribeSyncRemote`'s
six literals become `remoteTopology{sync: checkpointSyncInfo{...}}`; add a
dedicated case and a row-9 case. Then:

- **`TestDescribeCheckpointDestination`** (table, `t.Parallel()`) — first coverage
  of that function:
  - single remote → empty output; all-pinned (row 8) → empty output
  - **row 7**: `colleague`/`origin`(pinned)/`upstream`, dedicated store. Want the
    3-remote list, the store slug, `Pushes to "origin"`; **absent** `right now`,
    `To pin one repository`
  - **row 9**: same remotes, `IgnoredStore` set, elected `origin`. Want
    `not in effect`, `settings.local.json`; absent `To pin one repository`
  - **row 6**: `origin` elected, `origin2` fans out → absent `pushes to 2 URLs`
  - **row 5**: elected remote fans out → present, `→` marker on URL 0
  - **row 10**: `Err` set + a fanning-out remote → `NOT syncing`, no URL block
- **`TestInspectRemoteTopology_DedicatedStore`** — a real temp repo via
  `setupTestRepo` / `writeSettings` / `testutil.AddRemote` (pattern at
  `status_test.go:2248-2273`), tracked `settings.json` with
  `{"provider":"github","repo":"org/checkpoints"}`, `origin` = `github.com/org/repo`
  (owner match → pinned), plus two foreign remotes. Asserts the real end-to-end
  note. This is the test that would have caught the finding; the literal tables
  cannot, because they hand-build the state the bug is about.
- **Status, row 9**: extend `TestRunStatus_CheckpointSyncDedicated_IneligibleFallsBackToElected`
  (`status_test.go:2400`) and `TestRunStatusJSON_CheckpointSync_DedicatedIneligible`
  (`:2430`) — they already build exactly this state and today assert only the
  fallback. Add the new line and the new JSON field.

## Verification

```bash
go test ./cmd/entire/cli -run 'TestRunStatus_CheckpointSync|TestRunStatusJSON_CheckpointSync|TestDescribeSyncRemote|TestDescribeCheckpointDestination|TestInspectRemoteTopology'
go test -tags integration ./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test -run CheckpointSyncRemote
mise run fmt && mise run lint    # lint after fmt; see the repo's lint-binary caveat
mise run check
```

`entire status` must change in exactly one way — the new row-9 line and its JSON
field. Capture the output before and after on a repo with a dedicated store and
diff to confirm nothing else moved. Manual end-to-end:

```bash
# row 7 — store in effect
git remote add upstream https://github.com/entireio/cli.git
git remote add colleague https://github.com/someone/test-cli.git
# tracked .entire/settings.json: strategy_options.checkpoint_remote = {provider: github, repo: <you>/checkpoints}
entire doctor      # store named, origin listed, no "right now \"origin\""
entire status      # unchanged: dedicated checkpoint remote (<you>/checkpoints)

# row 9 — same settings.json, but origin owned by someone else
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/someone-else/app.git
entire doctor      # "configured but not in effect", checkpoints go to origin
entire status      # the ! line, and still "Checkpoints sync to: origin"

# row 6 — fan-out on a non-elected remote
git remote set-url --add --push origin2 https://github.com/you/test-cli2
entire doctor      # no URL block for origin2 while origin is elected
```

## Out of scope

The `ambiguous()` gate; a malformed `checkpoint_remote` entry (also silently
ignored — worth its own finding); and the dismissed finding `01M0F4K9Y8WR` (the
`SyncRemoteSourceSole` wording), which stays unreachable — the new single-remote
test case pins that.

## Context

`entire enable` and `entire doctor` print a "checkpoint destination" note

where checkpoints land. The note makes three independent claims — a per-remote
push-URL breakdown, a remote list, and a sync-destination line — and **none of
them consults the election** except the last, which consults it but ignores
`pinned`.

Trail #1108 finding `01M0FJ6N8PS0` reports one instance: when the elected remote
is pinned by a `checkpoint_remote` store, the note names a remote that is absent
from the list it just printed and is not where checkpoints go, while `entire
